summary: Defines the MIME Multipart/Related content type, used for compound documents in which parts such as images belong together with a main part, and gives examples of its use.

plainLanguage.summary: A package in which a main document and its pictures stay together, so the document can show its pictures.

questions: what is the start parameter in multipart/related
what is a content-id in mime
subtitle: One MIME mechanism for bundling a main document with the parts that only make sense together with it.

tldr.problem: Some objects, such as a document with its pictures, only make sense when all their body parts travel together, but each new kind of object was getting its own multipart subtype.
tldr.mechanism: Multipart/Related groups the parts into one entity. A required type parameter names the root part's media type, an optional start parameter points at the root by content-ID, and an optional start-info parameter carries extra processing information.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 2112 as the single mechanism for compound objects. Agents that do not know it treat the entity as Multipart/Mixed.

today: RFC 2387 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2112, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The only change from RFC 2112 the text records is that cid URLs were corrected to follow RFC 2111, with the angle brackets removed.

sections.title: Why a Related Type
sections.content:
Several uses of MIME, including MIME-PEM and MIME-Macintosh, need several body parts that make sense only as a group. Until now each new compound object got its own multipart subtype. RFC 2387 defines Multipart/Related as one shared mechanism instead, in keeping with the MIME idea of one mechanism for the same goal.

The object is categorized by a type parameter. Other parameters name a starting body part, called the root, and give auxiliary information for unpacking or processing. The application that handles the compound object, not the mail reader, is responsible for displaying or processing the parts.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing a new kind of box every time, there is one box for things that belong together, with a label saying what is inside.

sections.title: The Type, Start and Start-Info Parameters
sections.content:
The media type is intended for objects where proper display cannot be achieved by showing each body part on its own. The relationships between parts are often links inside the parts that point at other parts. Inside one machine those links are often file names; in a MIME message they can be content-IDs or the values of other Content- headers.

The type parameter is required. Its value is the media type of the root part, so a user agent can learn the content-type without looking inside. If it differs from the root part's own content-type, the user agent's behavior is undefined.

The start parameter, if given, is the content-ID of the root, the element the application processes first. Without it, the root is the first body part. The start-info parameter carries a string or a content-ID reference to another entity, for example extra command line parameters. Applications that use Multipart/Related must specify how start-info is interpreted, and a first non-white-space character of < marks a reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The label says what the main item is. You can also point at the main item by name, and add a note saying how to use it.

sections.title: Parameter Syntax
sections.content:
The three parameters may appear in any order. A start value is a cid, which is a message ID as in RFC 822. A start-info value is either a list of such IDs or a plain token or quoted string that cannot begin with <. The type value is a type and subtype separated by a slash.

Parameter values usually need quoting. A message ID contains special characters such as <, > and @, any quote marks inside it must be escaped, and the slash in the type parameter is also special.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the names contain odd symbols, you wrap them in quotes so nobody gets confused where a name starts and ends.

sections.title: Content-Disposition and Older Mail Readers
sections.content:
A Content-Disposition header suggests how to present a part, as INLINE or ATTACHMENT, and may give a file name. Adding it to parts of a Multipart/Related entity helps user agents that do not know the type, because they treat the entity as Multipart/Mixed and can use that hint.

When the application processing the compound object decides presentation for all parts, the disposition type is redundant or even misleading. So user agents that understand Multipart/Related shall ignore the disposition type in its parts. They may still pass the optional filename parameter to the application, depending on that application's rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Old readers that do not know the lunchbox just lay everything out on the table. New readers ignore the table hints and follow the lunchbox rules.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The first example is an invented Application/X-FixedRecord type. Its root lists, one number per line, how many octets of the octet-stream part make up each record. The root is chosen with start, the data part is base64 encoded, and start-info is "-o ps".

The second is an invented markup language, Text/x-Okie, whose text refers to two JPEG pictures by content-ID using cid:. The RFC notes that cid: is useful but not part of the Multipart/Related specification. A third example adds Content-Disposition: INLINE to an image part, which Multipart/Related-aware agents ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: One example is a list saying how to cut a long strip into pieces. Another is a story whose pictures are tucked into the same package.

sections.title: What User Agents Must Do
sections.content:
Agents that do not recognize Multipart/Related shall treat it as Multipart/Mixed. Agents that recognize it but cannot process the given type should let the user suppress the whole entity. Handling it differs from other multiparts because it cannot be reduced to handling the parts one by one.

A mail user agent is required to give the application the bodies and their Content- headers, the parameters of the Multipart/Related header, and the correspondence between each body's local file name, its header data and, if present, its content-ID. A nested Multipart/Related entity is processed as though it were being stored. The RFC also suggests that agents with configuration mechanisms name the type as Multipart/Related/<type>.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail program must hand over every piece, its label and where it was saved. If it cannot use the package, it should let you throw the whole thing away.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content: The registration form lists the media type as Multipart/Related with a required Type parameter and optional Start and Start-info parameters. Multipart content-types cannot have encodings. The security considerations are identical to those of the underlying content-type, which depends solely on the referenced type.
sections.plainLanguage: The package is only as safe as what is inside it, so the same care applies as for the main item.

viz.caption: SHORTENED FROM THE RFC 2387 FIXEDRECORD EXAMPLE

data.title: Multipart/Related header
data.code:
Content-Type: Multipart/Related; boundary=example-1
        start="<950120.aaCC@XIson.com>";
        type="Application/X-FixedRecord"
        start-info="-o ps"

--example-1
Content-Type: Application/X-FixedRecord
Content-ID: <950120.aaCC@XIson.com>
...
